svg.aria-label: Diagram: emergency access or break-glass accounts in Microsoft Entra, showing the five documented lockout scenarios these accounts exist for, the configuration requirements including cloud-only accounts on the onmicrosoft.com domain with permanent active Global Administrator and phishing-resistant credentials different from normal admin accounts, which Conditional Access policies need an exclusion and which do not, and the ninety-day validation drill
svg.title: The account that must work when every control in this phase has failed
svg.text: The account that must work when every control in this phase has failed.
Which means it must not depend on any of them — not the identity provider, not the phone, not PIM, not a person.
Five documented ways to be locked out of your own tenant
Federation is down
Entra redirects to your identity provider, and it does not answer
MFA is unreachable
a cell outage, and calls and texts were the only two methods registered
The last admin leaves
Entra blocks deleting the last Global Administrator, but “it doesn’t prevent
the account from being deleted or disabled on-premises”
A natural disaster
phones and networks unavailable at the same time
PIM eats itself
every admin eligible and none active, approval required, no approvers —
“no one can approve activation and tenant administration is effectively locked”
What the account must be
Two or more, cloud-only, on the *.onmicrosoft.com
domain, never federated or synced from on-premises.
Global Administrator, permanent active — not eligible.
The one place this series says never to use PIM.
Passkey (FIDO2) recommended, or certificate-based
auth — and deliberately a different method from the
one your normal admin accounts use.
Not tied to any individual. Not on anyone’s phone.
“must not expire or be in scope of automated cleanup”
Which policies need the exclusion
Exclude from Conditional Access policies that block or
restrict sign-in — via a dedicated group, not by name.
“Report-only policies don’t block access and don’t need
to exclude emergency accounts.”
The credential is what protects the account. The
exclusion only removes a policy that could “prevent
sign-in during the exact emergency the account is
designed for”.
Mandatory MFA is not excludable. See below.
The exclusion that no longer exists
“Break glass or emergency access accounts are also required to sign in with MFA once enforcement begins.” And on exceptions:
“The system enforcement applies to all user accounts, regardless if they are a student account, break-glass account, an
administrator account with activated or eligible roles, or any user exclusions that are enabled for them.”
A Conditional Access exclusion does not reach it — the enforcement sits on the Azure Resource Manager side. Which is why the
guidance moved to passkeys and certificates: they satisfy MFA without depending on a phone, a network, or a person.
Every 90 days, and it is a drill rather than a check
Tell the monitoring team first
the alert should fire — that is half of what is being tested
Sign in and do administrative work
not just authenticate — confirm the role actually functions
Re-read the authorised list
and change the safe combinations when someone leaves
Check no personal device crept in
no MFA or SSPR registered “to any individual user’s device”
Two independent network paths
paths that “don’t share a common failure mode” — wifi and cell
And afterwards: “If you used an emergency access account, remember to regenerate credentials” — the account is single-use by
convention, and every use gets a post-mortem asking whether it was a drill, a real emergency, or misuse.
Sources: Manage emergency access admin accounts, Plan for mandatory multifactor authentication, and Create a resilient access control management strategy, on Microsoft Learn.
